comments.text:
Good video with all things ok, except AGGREGATE DEDUCTIBLE. Please ask yourself - why are you buying health insurance? To pay most of your hospitalization bills yourself? Or wanting the insurer to pay those bills in place of you?

I guess we all have the same answer. So imho, NEVER opt for any aggregate deductible. It is just like a brother of co-pay, but worse. Maybe also worse than your claim not getting settled fully unfairly.

Yes, you get huge premium discount, but only if you take huge deductible. If you take 5 lakh deductible (which btw is a whole policy in itself for millions in India), you're getting 24k discount. Nice! But now even if you get one claim in of 5 lakh in 5 years, which is a good probability, you'll still have to pay all that 5 lakh yourself. So in these 5 years:
Amount you paid to insurer = 1.2 lakh,
Amount you paid to hospital = 5 lakh, and
Amount insurer paid for you = 0.
Who won?
And what if you've 4 claims of 4L each in these 5 years? L O L.
You'll be on profit only if your total claims in 5 years is less than 1.2 lakh, of which probability is really low.

Now even if the deductible was 1 lakh, so what?

In the beginning, I mentioned 'most of your hospitalization bills', because I'm assuming that most of your claims would be actually less than 5 lakhs in a year, unless you identify yourself as rishtedaar of Ambani or bollywood celebs or other top businessmen and go only to top expensive hospitals. But that doesn't mean u buy small SI plans, because 10L cover maybe an okay amount today for 99% Indians, it would not be okay 10 years from now.

PS: nobody needs to take anything personally. By 'you/your', I mean general people reading the comment, and not just OP Pranay.

comments.text: This was a very helpful video. Thank you, Pranay. While comparing claim settlement ratio, incurred claim ratio, and complaint ratio, I think one nuance everyone is missing is whether it's a general insurance company vs health insurance company, and what's the distribution of their business. If you're a general insurance company mostly doing life insurance, your claim settlement ratio should be very high and complaints ratio quite low, as there are far fewer reasons to reject such claims, and they happen at most once in the lifetime of a policy. However, standalone health insurance are likely to have a lower claim settlement ratio and higher complaints ratio due to nature of the products. Furthermore, for a new insurer like Aditya Birla, isn't it expected that their incurred claim ratio will remain low initially and increase slowly? It seems unlikely that users will start making claims immediately after taking up new policies unless their underwriting is below average. Thoughts?

comments.text: Can you explain what is Aggregate deductable?
comments.author: @sanskarkhaitan404

comments.text:
Think of it like a yearly allowance you have to pay for your own medical bills before your insurance kicks in.

Let's say your aggregate deductible is ₹2 lakhs.

You're responsible for paying the first ₹2 lakhs of your medical expenses in a year.
It doesn't matter if that ₹2 lakhs comes from one big bill or several smaller bills throughout the year.
Once you've paid that ₹2 lakhs, your insurance starts covering the rest (according to your policy, of course).
So, if you have a ₹5 lakh bill, you pay ₹2 lakhs, and insurance pays ₹3 lakhs. If you have several smaller bills that add up to ₹2 lakhs, you pay those, and then insurance pays for any further eligible expenses.

The key word "aggregate" just means it's a total amount across all your claims in a year, not a deductible that applies to each separate claim.
